title: The Pleasure of Amateurs
sentences: There was once a certain dignity in being merely competent at something purely for its own sake.
Now even a modest hobby quickly attracts advice, rankings, and the pressure to keep improving.
An amateur, in the old sense, loved a pursuit because nothing serious hung on the outcome.
That freedom is increasingly rare, since almost any pastime can now be measured and compared.
To play badly and still enjoy it has come to seem faintly embarrassing, even a little wasteful.
And yet mastery, chased too earnestly, can quietly drain the pleasure that first drew someone in.
Futility, oddly enough, is part of the appeal of practising a skill nobody will ever reward.
Precisely because it leads nowhere, a private hobby can remain a small, untouched refuge.
Arguably, we need pursuits that resist improvement, or at least refuse to be judged by it.
To potter about badly, unwatched and unranked, may be one of the last quiet luxuries left.
